To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the proportion of patients with alarm symptoms diagnosed with either cancer diagnoses or non-cancer diseases is generally high, and that for every four to seven presentations of alarm symptoms, a cancer or non-cancers diagnosis is identified.
the majority of patients who present with alarm symptoms are not found to have cancer, but that clinically relevant diagnoses are made for a substantial proportion of patients.
the proportion diagnosed with either a cancer or a non-cancer diagnosis generally increased with age and was 14% to 25% within 90 days of presentation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of cancer in primary care.
the development and validation of a new diagnostic tool, the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale.
the identification and management of patients presenting with symptoms that might indicate a serious underlying disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of any alarm symptom in the absence of a clear explanation is associated with a high risk of cancer or other serious conditions.
alarm symptoms in primary care should not be considered as a single entity but rather a set of symptoms that may have a wide spectrum of underlying diagnoses.
the presence of alarm symptoms in primary care patients is associated with a high likelihood of a non-cancer diagnosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that alarm symptoms have predictive value for both cancer and non-cancer diagnoses.
alarm symptoms are common in patients presenting with alarm symptom and that the proportion of patients with a cancer diagnosis is small.
alarm symptoms have a low specificity for cancer but a high positive predictive value for relevant non-cancer diagnoses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with alarm symptoms are at high risk for a wide variety of non-cancer diseases, and that the risk is even higher in older patients.
the majority of patients presenting with an alarm symptom are not found to have cancer.
patients presenting with alarm features should be evaluated for both non-cancer and cancer diagnoses, and that the evaluation should not be limited by a fixed time period.
